fields.rationale: States cluster around how demanding and specific their reciprocity conditions are: some defer almost entirely to board discretion or say little beyond good standing and equivalent standards, while others layer on active practice minimums (ranging 1–5 years), mandatory jurisprudence exams, NBEO proof, CE verification, and disciplinary checks — producing a spectrum from minimal to strict multi-condition bundles.

assignments.raw_value: Applicant must be a graduate of a board-recognized optometry school; pass Alaska laws/regulations exam; hold a current equivalent license in another US state/territory or Canadian province; have previously passed the NBEO; have at least 3,120 hours of active licensed clinical practice in the preceding 36 months; no disciplinary history; and have adequate education in pain management and opioid use (unless no DEA registration).

Must have passed a standard optometry examination in another state or the full NBEO examination, hold a current license in another state, have practiced ethically for at least one year, pay the regular examination fee, and pass the Alabama standard examination at the board's discretion.

Applicant must be qualified under Arkansas chapter, hold a license from a state with standards at least equal to Arkansas, have practiced lawfully for 3 of the past 4 years, pass an Arkansas jurisprudence exam, submit transcripts, certifications, NBEO proof, criminal background check, and pay applicable fees.

Licensure by endorsement requires: (1) a valid license from another US jurisdiction with equivalent requirements; (2) no suspension or revocation in any other jurisdiction for causes that would be grounds in AZ; (3) continuous practice in that jurisdiction or US military for at least 4 of the 5 years preceding the application; (4) successful verification by board-designated national data banks.

Applicant must hold a doctor of optometry degree from an accredited school, have passed the licensing examination in another state, be currently licensed in good standing in all states where licensed, meet CE requirements for current and preceding year, have met TPA certification requirements, pass the California jurisprudence examination, and satisfy other requirements.

Applicant must satisfy the requirements of the occupational credential portability program under section 12-20-202(3), including demonstration of substantially equivalent experience or credentials and holding a current valid license in good standing from another jurisdiction for at least one year with a substantially similar scope of practice.

fields.rationale: States cluster by how broadly controlled substances and oral agents are permitted: some allow Sched III–V plus hydrocodone (often Sched II), some allow Sched III–V without hydrocodone carve-outs, some restrict to limited oral plus topical agents, some rely on board formularies or rules to define scope, some are effectively diagnostic/topical only, and several use tiered certification structures to expand authority incrementally.

Optometrists approved by the board may prescribe and administer pharmaceutical agents (diagnostic and therapeutic drugs) for the human eye and adjacent structures, including steroids, Schedule III-V controlled substances (excluding Schedule I and II narcotics and Schedule III agents containing Hydrocodone), and Schedule III agents limited to 96-hour prescriptions; may administer epinephrine/benadryl for anaphylaxis.

Licensed optometrists (with board certification) may possess, administer, and prescribe all oral and topical drugs for diagnosis or treatment of conditions of the eye, lids, and adnexa, and epinephrine/benadryl for anaphylaxis. Therapeutically certified optometrists may administer and prescribe therapeutic pharmaceutical agents for prevention, management, or treatment of conditions and diseases of the eye and ocular adnexa, subject to restrictions (no controlled dangerous substances, no intravenous delivery, no injections except epinephrine for anaphylaxis, certain systemic agents prohibited). Certified optometrists may prescribe and use therapeutic pharmaceutical agents for conditions of the eye and eyelids, excluding Schedule I drugs, intraocular injections/implants, and dermal fillers/cosmetic injectables. Diagnostic pharmaceutical agents (anesthetics, mydriatics, cycloplegics, dyes, OTC drugs) authorized for certified optometrists. Anaphylaxis auto-injection (epi-pen) authorized. Licensed optometrists may administer, dispense, and prescribe oral analgesics (codeine, propoxyphene, hydrocodone, dihydrocodeine) and drugs approved by the board for ocular treatment limited to the anterior segment and adnexa; topical diagnostic agents including cycloplegics, mydriatics, anesthetics, fluorescein, and emergency miotics; glaucoma may be treated.

Optometrists certified by the Board may prescribe and use pharmaceutical agents in the practice of optometry; licensed druggists may fill such prescriptions. Optometrists certified by the board may prescribe and use pharmaceutical agents including diagnostic and therapeutic agents (topical, locally administered, oral anti-infectives, antihistaminics, and oral analgesics). Optometrists may not dispense therapeutic pharmaceutical agents except as drug samples or selling contact lenses/ophthalmic devices classified as drugs by FDA.

Controlled substance prescriptions must not exceed 90 MME/day and must not last more than 72 hours. Glaucoma treatment requires additional certification under NRS 636.2895.

Optometrists certified by the department may use diagnostic pharmaceuticals, topical therapeutic pharmaceutical agents, therapeutic pharmaceutical agents for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, and oral therapeutic pharmaceutical agents, all within certified categories and FDA-approved availability. Use of drugs is authorized only in accordance with this article and commissioner's regulations.

Licensed optometrists may employ, apply, administer, and prescribe topical ocular pharmaceutical agents and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents (including oral anti-infectives, anti-allergy agents, antiglaucoma agents, analgesics, anti-inflammatories, and other FDA-approved ophthalmic drugs), and may prescribe analgesic controlled substances to the extent authorized by board rules. Prescribing appropriate pharmaceutical agents for the diagnosis, management, and treatment of the eye and adnexa, including oral therapeutic pharmaceutical agents and topical agents for glaucoma management.

Licensed optometrists certified under the statute may use topical and oral drugs for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes; oral Schedule III through V controlled substances (and Schedule II hydrocodone combination products with board and pharmacy commission approval); may not prescribe Schedule I or II controlled substances except Schedule II hydrocodone combination products; controlled substances limited to 7 days per episode; oral corticosteroids beyond 7 days require physician consultation.

Optometrists may use topical ocular diagnostic pharmaceutical agents (with board certification or license issued on or after August 1, 2006) and therapeutic pharmaceutical agents (with board certification or license issued on or after August 1, 2006). Specific agents are specified by rule promulgated by the secretary after consultation with the examining board, medical examining board, and pharmacy examining board. Optometrists may not dispense therapeutic agents except by prescribing or administering, or providing complimentary samples, or dispensing a therapeutic-delivering contact lens.

A licensee with a certificate may administer or prescribe topical pharmaceutical agents for the anterior segment and drugs from the board-established formulary including oral drugs from Schedules III, IV, and V, oral antibiotics, NSAIDs, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. May not use Schedule II controlled substances except an oral pharmaceutical certified licensee may prescribe hydrocodone for no more than three days.

An optometrist shall be allowed to administer and prescribe pharmaceutical agents related to the practice of optometry for the treatment of ocular disease, excluding schedule I and II narcotics, but allowing for the prescribing of hydrocodone or hydrocodone containing pharmaceutical agents regardless of schedule.

fields.rationale: States cluster by how they define surgery: those with broad 'tissue cut/altered/infiltrated' language, those anchoring on 'invasive procedure' framing, those that list specific prohibited procedures rather than defining surgery abstractly, those that simply exclude surgery without defining it, and those that key on suture closure or anesthesia requirements as the definitional marker.

Invasive surgery including injections into the eyeball, cataract surgery, muscle surgery, retinal surgery, radial keratotomy, laser surgery, and cryosurgery.

Surgery of the lid, adnexa, or visual system which requires anything other than a topical anesthetic is excluded from the practice of optometry; also specifically excluded are cataract surgery and radial keratotomy surgery.

An invasive procedure in which in vivo human tissue is cut, burned, vaporized, removed, coagulated or photodisrupted by use of an electrical cautery, a scalpel, a cryoprobe, a laser or ionizing radiation. Surgery does not include nonsurgical procedures, including the removal of superficial foreign bodies or eyelashes or the use of lasers for diagnostic purposes.

Any act in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by any means. It does not mean an act that solely involves the administration or prescribing of a topical or oral therapeutic pharmaceutical.
Surgery means any procedure in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by mechanical or laser means

The practice of advanced optometric care does not include surgical treatment of glaucoma, treatment of ocular cancer, treatment of infectious diseases of the retina, surgical procedures other than noninvasive procedures, procedures that require the cutting or opening of the globe, enucleation of the eye, extraocular muscle surgery or any invasive procedure performed on the human body other than noninvasive procedures performed on the eye or ocular adnexae.

Surgery includes use of ophthalmic lasers or other modalities in which tissue is burned, vaporized, cut, or otherwise irreversibly altered by thermal, light-based, electromagnetic, radiation, chemical, ultrasound, infusion, cryotherapy, or similar means; also includes anterior corneal stromal puncture, collagen cross-linking, postsurgical pterygium or conjunctival graft gluing of amniotic membranes, mechanical polishing of the corneal basement membrane, or any procedure that requires full- or partial-thickness incision of the sclera or cornea.

A procedure using an instrument, including a laser, scalpel, or needle, in which human tissue is cut, burned, scraped except as provided in s. 463.014(4), or vaporized, by incision, injection, ultrasound, laser, infusion, cryotherapy, or radiation. The term includes a procedure using an instrument which requires the closure of human tissue by suture, clamp, or other such device.
Surgery is excluded from optometric practice, including refractive or therapeutic laser surgery; invasive surgery is also not allowed for therapeutically certified optometrists.

Surgical procedures requiring injectable or general anesthesia, moderate sedation, penetration of the globe, or use of ophthalmic lasers for ophthalmic surgery within or upon the globe; specifically prohibited are removal of pterygia and Salzmann's nodules, incisional corneal refractive surgery, and strabismus surgery.

Surgery is not defined in the statute beyond the prohibition language, but the practice of optometry shall not include the performance of surgery, including the use of lasers for surgical purposes, and shall not include procedures requiring anesthesia administered by injection or general anesthesia.

Excluded nonlaser and laser surgical procedures include: removal of the eye, full thickness incision/excision of cornea or sclera (other than emergency paracentesis), penetrating/lamellar keratoplasty, incision of iris and ciliary body, incision of vitreous, incision of retina, surgical extraction of crystalline lens, intraocular implants, extraocular muscle surgery, eyelid surgery for malignancies or incisional cosmetic/mechanical repair, bony orbit surgery, lacrimal system incisional/excisional surgery (other than probing), full thickness conjunctivoplasty with graft or flap, any nonlaser su

A procedure upon the human eye in which in vivo human tissue is injected, cut, burned, frozen, sutured, vaporized, coagulated, or photodisrupted by the use of surgical instrumentation such as, but not limited to, a scalpel, cryoprobe, laser, electric cautery, or ionizing radiation.
invasive surgical procedures

a procedure using any instruments, including lasers, scalpels, needles, cautery, a cryoprobe, or sutures in which human tissue is cut, burned, vaporized, removed, or otherwise permanently altered by any mechanical means, laser, ionizing radiation, ultrasound, or other means
Invasive surgery is excluded from the practice of optometry; tissue-altering lasers are also excluded.

'Invasive procedures' means: (i) the use of lasers other than for observation; (ii) the use of ionizing radiation; (iii) the use of therapeutic ultrasound; (iv) the administration of medication by injection; (v) procedures that include an incision.
invasive surgery including, but not limited to, surgery using lasers

Intraocular surgical procedures (including cataract surgery) are prohibited; procedures requiring intraocular injection, intraocular implantation, biopsy of any part of the globe, or intraocular aspiration or penetration are excluded from optometric scope.
Surgery is excluded from the definition of optometric practice; the statute does not further define surgery but excludes it from authorized methods in both examination and treatment
invasive surgery
Surgery and laser surgery are excluded from the practice of optometry; the treatment of infantile/congenital glaucoma (present at birth) is also excluded.

any procedure in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by mechanical means, including use of lasers for therapeutic and photorefractive purposes, ionizing radiation, therapeutic ultrasound, or medication administered by injection

Surgery is excluded from optometric practice except for enumerated in-office minor surgical procedures; the general prohibition covers 'the use of surgery or injections in the treatment of eye diseases' beyond those specifically listed.

Any procedure using a laser, scalpel, needle or other instrument in which any human tissue is cut, burned or vaporized by incision, injection, ultrasound, laser, infusion, cryotherapy, radiation or other means; or any procedure using an instrument which requires the closure of human tissue by suture, clamp or similar device.

Surgery is an invasive modality, meaning any procedure in which human tissue is cut, altered, or otherwise infiltrated by mechanical or other means; invasive modality includes surgery, lasers, ionizing radiation, therapeutic ultrasound and the removal of foreign bodies from within the tissue of the eye.

An invasive procedure means any procedure that involves cutting or otherwise infiltrating human tissue by mechanical means including surgery, laser surgery, ionizing radiation, therapeutic ultrasound, administering medication by injection, or the removal of intraocular foreign bodies.
Invasive or laser surgery is excluded from the practice of optometry by definition.

Surgery includes, but is not limited to, diagnostic, exploratory, palliative, therapeutic, rehabilitative, cosmetic, reconstructive, refractive, light-based or laser surgery; or the use of lasers for therapeutic purposes.

Surgery is not explicitly defined, but the statute bars any 'surgery or other invasive techniques' in treatment of eye conditions and prohibits surgery 'for the purpose of detecting any diseased or pathological condition of the eye'.

Surgery includes, but is not limited to, an invasive procedure using instruments that require closure by suturing, clamping, or other similar devices or a procedure in which the presence or assistance of a nurse anesthetist or an anesthesiologist is required.

Surgeries are excluded from the general 'any means or method' for correction of visual process abnormalities, unless otherwise permitted by this chapter; intraocular surgery and refractive surgery are explicitly prohibited; selective laser trabeculoplasty and posterior capsulotomy by YAG laser are permitted under expanded scope with board authorization.
Surgical procedures requiring other than a topical anesthetic; cataract surgery; radial keratotomy; reconstructive surgical procedures on the eyelid; use of nondiagnostic ophthalmic lasers

A procedure using instruments, including lasers, scalpels, or needles, in which human tissue is cut, burned, vaporized, or otherwise altered by any mechanical means, laser, or ionizing radiation. Includes procedures requiring closing by suturing, clamping, or another device. Does not include a noninvasive procedure to remove a superficial foreign body in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or corneal epithelium that has not perforated the Bowman's membrane.
Surgery in which human tissue is cut, burned, or vaporized by means of laser or ionizing radiation (as applied to laser surgery); broader surgery prohibition also applies

For purposes of the subtitle, 'surgery' means the structural alteration of the human body by the incision or cutting into of tissue for the purpose of diagnostic or therapeutic treatment of conditions or disease processes by any instrument causing localized alteration or transposition of live human tissue, but does not include procedures for the removal of superficial foreign bodies, punctures, injections, dry needling, acupuncture, or removal of dead tissue.

Any invasive procedure in which human tissue is cut, ablated, or otherwise penetrated by incision, injection, laser, ultrasound, or other means, in order to: treat human eye diseases; alter or correct refractive error; or alter or enhance cosmetic appearance.
Surgery is not defined in the statute, but the practice of optometry expressly excludes 'surgery or medical treatment' except as provided within the defined scope of optometry.
